about: Descriptions shown when a catalogue row or an election is opened, on a map's Details page and on an election's Browse page. Keyed by catalogue series id (rows) and election key (elections). Built into data/catalogue/catalogue.json (as about) and Browse's election records by scripts/catalogue/build-catalogue.mjs and scripts/build-browse-indexes.mjs; checked by scripts/catalogue/check-catalogue.mjs.
source: Phelim Birch, Civgraph descriptions document (Google Doc 13JPxXeZxjXDqv_JIlmxtAWDZeT_8GEOqfHPbl121THo), as of 2026-10-12; 13 further Dáil general elections from his Word document 'Civgraph Catalogue Descriptions' (2026-10-18). 1954 and 1957 as Phelim revised them, 2026-10-19. New local, European, presidential and referendum descriptions, and 1997 and 2016 Dáil revisions, from the same Google Doc as of 2026-10-24 (four factual slips corrected: 1984 vote shares, 2014 Sinn Féin seat share, 1987 and 2011 Wikipedia links; and, on review, the Nice II common-defence clause, Ó Dálaigh’s dispute with the government, O’Kelly’s 1945 final share on the valid-poll basis, Robinson as an independent nominated by Labour, and the Socialist Group in 1979 and 1989). The 2001 referendums and the 2025 presidential election added from the same document, 2026-10-24.

text: Townlands are the smallest territorial division that cover the entirety of Ireland, and are grouped to make up larger areas such as civil parishes and electoral divisions. Townland boundaries have changed little over the centuries.
For an online index of digitally mapped townlands, see the Townlands.ie project.

Civil parishes (not to be confused with Catholic parishes or Church of Ireland parishes) are small territorial divisions that were used for administrative purposes before the advent of poor law unions and electoral divisions in the 19th century. Civil parishes are grouped to make up baronies, and both are occasionally used today for legal purposes.

links.label: Wikipedia: List of civil parishes of Ireland

text: Baronies are historical subdivisions of counties. They largely stopped being used for administrative purposes following the Local Government (Ireland) Act 1898, and their boundaries (maritime boundaries excluded) have not changed since.

links.label: Wikipedia: List of baronies of Ireland

text: The traditional counties of Ireland, which date back to the Norman conquest, are used as a basis for administrative counties and parliamentary constituencies. They are also notably used by the GAA, which still treats county boundaries as they were at its foundation in 1884. County boundaries have significantly changed over the centuries, with the modern boundaries being based on their corresponding administrative counties.

The four provinces of Ireland are purely cultural (and not administrative) regions made up of groups of counties. They are based on historical kingdoms and (much like the counties that make them up) their boundaries have significantly changed over the centuries, with the modern boundaries being based on administrative counties.

Catholic parishes (not to be confused with civil parishes) are the smallest territorial division used by the Catholic Church and typically centre around a single church/priest. Parishes are grouped together to make dioceses. As of now, our map only contains parishes within the diocese of Dublin.

Dioceses are large territorial divisions made up of groups of parishes and centred around a bishop. Ireland has 26 Catholic dioceses, two of which are wholly in Northern Ireland and four of which have territory on both sides of the border.

links.label: Wikipedia: List of Catholic dioceses in Ireland

text: Peacelines (also known as peace walls) are physical barriers, built from 1969 onwards, to separate predominantly unionist neighbourhoods from nationalist ones in Northern Ireland. They were intended to reduce the risk of inter-communal violence, but have been criticised for segregating communities.
Municipal districts are local authorities that are a tier below county councils. They were established in 2014 to replace town councils and are defined based on local electoral areas.

links.label: Wikipedia: Local electoral area § Municipal districts

text: Administrative counties, also known as local authorities or council areas, are the areas represented by the Republic of Ireland’s county and city councils. They are the same as the traditional counties with the exceptions of Cork and Galway being split into city and county and Dublin being split into its city and three separate counties.

links.label: Wikipedia: Local government in the Republic of Ireland

text: Local Government Districts are the areas covered by Northern Ireland’s 11 District Councils. They were formed in 2015, following mergers of the 26 councils which were formed in 1973.

links.label: Wikipedia: Local government in Northern Ireland § Local government districts (since 2015)

text: The two polities on the island of Ireland: the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.
Divisions of the Republic of Ireland used by the Garda Síochána.

Health and Social Care Trusts are organisations which administer the healthcare system in five major regions of Northern Ireland, similar in shape to the Education and Library Boards. They were formed in 2007, following the merger of the old 19 health and social services trusts.

links.label: Wikipedia: Health and Social Care (Northern Ireland) § Trusts

text: Areas of the Republic of Ireland legally defined as being predominantly Irish-speaking.
Areas represented by the Republic of Ireland’s city councils and town councils before two of the former (Limerick and Waterford) and all of the latter were abolished in 2014.

links.label: Wikipedia: City status in Ireland § Republic of Ireland

text: Administrative areas were the local authorities of Northern Ireland prior to the formation of the 26 unitary District Councils in 1973. They consisted of a lower tier of Urban Districts, Municipal Boroughs (both covering towns), Rural Districts (covering countryside areas); an upper tier of Administrative Counties; and the two County Boroughs, Belfast and Londonderry, which were unitary authorities with the powers of both tiers.

The administrative counties consisted of the county boroughs of Belfast and Londonderry, plus the six other administrative counties of Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry and Tyrone, which are almost the same as the traditional counties, except for the areas covered by the two county boroughs. Today, these areas have no administrative function, and are only used for ceremonial purposes as the Lieutenancy areas. The boundaries of the administrative counties saw no changes after 1915.

Ireland’s administrative counties were set up under the Local Government (Ireland) Act 1898 and were based on the preceding system of judicial counties. These administrative counties, with a few modifications, are still used in the Republic of Ireland today, and were used in Northern Ireland until 1973.

The Education and Library Boards were set up in the early 1970s following the Macrory Report into public administration. They covered five regions of Northern Ireland, made up of combinations of Local Government Districts. The Boards were abolished in 2015, and became regions of the unified Education Authority.

links.label: Wikipedia: Education in Northern Ireland § Administration

text: Electoral divisions (EDs) are small areas used for statistical reporting and creating electoral constituencies such as Dáil constituencies and local electoral areas. Before 1996, EDs in cities were known as wards and EDs outside of cities were known as district electoral divisions.

Electoral Wards are the basic unit of political representation in Northern Ireland today. Historically, they were the units of Urban Districts and Municipal Boroughs, each electing one or more councillors. Since 1973, they have been formed by subdividing Local Government Districts, and have served as the building blocks of the District Electoral Areas (which elect one councillor for each ward they have), and of the Parliamentary Constituencies.

links.label: Wikipedia: Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom § Northern Ireland

text: Local electoral areas are subdivisions of administrative counties used for city/county council elections. Their boundaries are usually redrawn for every set of local elections.

District Electoral Areas are the basic unit of representation in Local Government Districts. Each elects 5, 6 or 7 councillors, depending on whether they have 5, 6 or 7 Wards (before 1985, some DEAs had 4 or 8 Councillors/Wards). DEAs are the most granular unit in Northern Ireland for which election results are available.

links.label: Wikipedia: Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom § Northern Ireland

text: Subdivisions of the Republic of Ireland used for elections to Dáil Éireann. Their boundaries are usually redrawn after every census. Each constituency elects 3, 4 or 5 Teachtaí Dála (with constituencies of up to 9 TDs existing historically).

Westminster Constituencies are the constituencies used for elections to the Parliament of the United Kingdom in Westminster. Each one elects 1 member (up to 2 prior to 1950), and covers a territorial area (or a university, prior to 1950).

links.label: Wikipedia: List of UK Parliament constituencies in Northern Ireland
Wikipedia: List of United Kingdom parliamentary constituencies in Ireland 1801–1885

text: Northern Ireland Constituencies are the constituencies used for the Northern Ireland Assembly and past devolved legislatures. Since 1973, these have always followed the Westminster constituencies, as was the case with the Northern Ireland Forum (1996), Northern Ireland Constitutional Convention (1975), the old Northern Ireland Assemblies (1973, 1982). The Parliament of Northern Ireland had its own constituencies until its disbandment in 1972, except for 1921 and 1925, when it used the Westminster constituencies.
Subdivisions of the Republic of Ireland (as well as the Northern Ireland constituency, which existed up until Brexit) for elections to the European Parliament.

links.label: Wikipedia: European Parliament constituencies in the Republic of Ireland

text: Polling districts used for elections and referendums in the Republic of Ireland.

District electoral divisions (DEDs) were used for elections to local authorities in Northern Ireland from its creation in 1921, until 1973 when they were all replaced with Wards. Each DED elected one or more councillors, either a single councillor serving a term of a few years, or three councillors serving three-year cycles and with one seat being up for election each year. In almost all cases in urban areas, DEDs were coterminous with Wards.

District electoral divisions (DEDs), which succeeded the previous system of poor law electoral divisions in 1899, were used for elections to rural district councils, as well as for statistical reporting and creating county electoral divisions. They were last used as constituencies in the 1914 local elections, having that purpose replaced by district electoral areas (themselves combinations of DEDs) by the next set of elections in 1920.

links.label: Wikipedia: Electoral division (Ireland) § History until partition

text: County electoral divisions were combinations of district electoral divisions, used to elect county councillors to administrative counties in Northern Ireland, prior to the abolition of the administrative counties in 1973.
County electoral divisions were combinations of district electoral divisions used for elections to the county council system established in 1899.

County Dublin was split into three “electoral counties”, groups of local electoral areas, in 1985 to prepare for the splitting of the county and its council into three new administrative counties, which happened in 1994.

In 2011, the UK held a referendum on the Alternative Vote (AV) system. While local authorities and devolved constituencies were used as the counting areas in England, Scotland and Wales, in Northern Ireland the results were reported based on ‘counting areas’, made up of combinations of 2-3 Westminster constituencies, while the turnout was reported based on the Westminster constituencies themselves.

links.label: Wikipedia: 2011 United Kingdom Alternative Vote referendum

text: Election for the 34th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 33rd Dáil’s tenure. A second Fianna Fáil-Fine Gael coalition government (swapping out the Green Party for a group of 9 independents) was elected, with Micheál Martin and Simon Harris being reappointed as rotating Taoisigh.

Election for the 33rd Dáil, triggered due to instability within the 32nd Dáil. An unprecedented Fianna Fáil-Fine Gael-Green Party coalition government was elected, with Micheál Martin and Leo Varadkar being appointed as rotating Taoisigh. Simon Harris was appointed as Taoiseach after Varadkar’s resignation in April 2024.

Election for the 32nd Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 31st Dáil’s tenure. A Fine Gael minority government (in coalition with 9 independents and in a confidence and supply arrangement with Fianna Fáil) was elected, with Enda Kenny being reappointed as Taoiseach. Leo Varadkar was appointed as Taoiseach after Kenny’s resignation in June 2017.

Election for the 31st Dáil, triggered due to economic downturn and the withdrawal of the Green Party from the ruling coalition. A Fine Gael-Labour coalition government was elected, with Enda Kenny being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 30th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 29th Dáil’s tenure. A Fianna Fáil-Green Party-Progressive Democrats coalition government (also including 4 independents) was elected, with Bertie Ahern being reappointed as Taoiseach. Brian Cowen was appointed as Taoiseach after Ahern’s resignation in May 2008. The Progressive Democrats dissolved in November 2009 (with its two TDs remaining in the coalition as independents), and the Green Party withdrew from the coalition in January 2011.

Election for the 29th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 28th Dáil’s tenure. A Fianna Fáil-Progressive Democrats coalition government was re-elected, with Bertie Ahern being reappointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 28th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 27th Dáil’s tenure. A Fianna Fáil-Progressive Democrats coalition minority government was elected, with Bertie Ahern being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 27th Dáil, triggered due to the withdrawal of the Progressive Democrats from the ruling coalition as a consequence of the Beef Tribunal. A Fianna Fáil-Labour coalition government was elected, with Albert Reynolds being reappointed as Taoiseach. The 1994 Irish government crisis resulted in Labour leaving the coalition in November 1994 and the Rainbow Coalition (Fine Gael-Labour-Democratic Left) being formed in December, with John Bruton being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 26th Dáil, triggered due to the defeat of the ruling government in a private members’ motion regarding the establishment of a fund for AIDS victims. A Fianna Fáil-Progressive Democrats coalition, Fianna Fáil’s first coalition government (and the start of a yet unbroken streak of coalition governments), was elected, with Charles Haughey being reappointed as Taoiseach. Albert Reynolds was appointed as Taoiseach after Haughey’s resignation in February 1992.

Election for the 25th Dáil, triggered due to the withdrawal of the Labour Party from the ruling coalition over budget proposal disagreements. A Fianna Fáil minority government was elected, with Charles Haughey being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 24th Dáil, triggered due to the ruling government losing a motion of confidence after a series of scandals (among them the Malcolm MacArthur affair). A Fine Gael-Labour coalition government was elected, with Garret FitzGerald being appointed as Taoiseach.
Election for the 23rd Dáil, triggered due to the ruling coalition’s budget proposal being voted down. A Fianna Fáil minority government was elected, with Charles Haughey being appointed as Taoiseach.
Election for the 22nd Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 21st Dáil’s tenure. A Fine Gael-Labour coalition minority government was elected, with Garret FitzGerald being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 21st Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 20th Dáil’s tenure. A Fianna Fáil government was elected, with Jack Lynch being appointed as Taoiseach. Charles Haughey was appointed as Taoiseach after Lynch’s resignation in December 1979.

Election for the 20th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 19th Dáil’s tenure. A Fine Gael-Labour coalition government was elected (the two parties had campaigned together under the “National Coalition” banner), with Liam Cosgrave being appointed as Taoiseach.
Election for the 19th Dáil, triggered due to the end of the 18th Dáil’s tenure. A Fianna Fáil government was elected, with Jack Lynch being reappointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 18th Dáil, triggered due to the loss of the ruling government in the 1965 Cork Mid bye-election. A Fianna Fáil government was elected, with Seán Lemass being reappointed as Taoiseach. Jack Lynch was appointed as Taoiseach after Lemass’s resignation in November 1966.

Election for the 17th Dáil, triggered due to discourse around Ireland’s application to join the European Economic Community and other international affairs. A Fianna Fáil minority government was elected, with Seán Lemass being reappointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 16th Dáil, triggered due to an impending vote of confidence in the ruling coalition. A Fianna Fáil government was elected, with Éamon de Valera being appointed as Taoiseach. Seán Lemass was appointed as Taoiseach after de Valera was elected as President in June 1959.

Election for the 15th Dáil, triggered due to a series of bye-election losses relating to the ruling government’s economic policies. A Fine Gael-Labour-Clann na Talmhan government (known as the Second Inter-Party Government) was elected, with John A. Costello being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 14th Dáil, triggered due to a series of crises (among them the Mother and Child Scheme). A Fianna Fáil minority government was elected, with Éamon de Valera being appointed as Taoiseach.

Election for the 13th Dáil, triggered due to the ruling party being threatened by the rise of Clann na Poblachta. A Fine Gael-Labour-Clann na Poblachta-Clann na Talmhan-National Labour Party coalition government (known as the First Inter-Party Government, and also including 1 independent) was elected, with John A. Costello being appointed as Taoiseach.
Referendum held on a potential 39th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have redefined family. The amendment was rejected with a 32.3% Yes / 67.7% No vote.

Referendum held on a potential 40th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have replaced an article on women’s “life within the home” and economic support for mothers with an article on care for family members and support for such care. The amendment was rejected with a 26.1% Yes / 73.9% No vote.

Referendum held on the 38th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which removed a required amount of time that partners needed to have been separated to get a divorce, explicitly permits laws recognising divorces under foreign law and removed a prohibition on divorcees who got a divorce under foreign law remarrying. The amendment was passed with a 82.1% Yes / 17.9% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-eighth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 37th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which removed a requirement to criminalise blasphemy. The amendment was passed with a 64.9% Yes / 35.1% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-seventh Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 36th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which repealed the 8th, 13th and 14th amendments that respectively guaranteed the unborn the right to life, stated that there was no limit to foreign travel and stated that there was no limit to obtaining or making available information on services in foreign countries. The new amendment was passed with a 66.4% Yes / 33.6% No vote, and all three existing amendments were replaced with explicit permission for laws regulating abortion.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-sixth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 34th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which explicitly permits same-sex marriage. The amendment was passed with a 62.1% Yes / 37.9% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-fourth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 35th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have reduced the presidential age of candidacy from 35 to 21. The amendment was rejected with a 26.9% Yes / 73.1% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-fifth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2015

text: Referendum held on the 33rd amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which established the Court of Appeal. The amendment was passed with a 65.2% Yes / 34.8% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-third Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 32nd amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have abolished the Seanad. The amendment was rejected with a 48.3% Yes / 51.7% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-second Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2013

text: Referendum held on the 31st amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which adds significantly more provisions for children’s rights. The amendment was passed with a 58.0% Yes / 42.0% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty-first Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 30th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the European Fiscal Compact. The amendment was passed with a 60.4% Yes / 39.6% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirtieth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 29th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which adds exceptions to the prohibition of reducing judge remuneration. The amendment was passed with a 79.7% Yes / 20.3% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-ninth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 30th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have provided for the Houses of the Oireachtas to conduct full inquiries. The amendment was rejected with a 46.7% Yes / 53.3% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirtieth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2011

text: Referendum held on the 28th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Treaty of Lisbon. Following the rejection of the similar amendment the year prior, EU member states issued Ireland a set of guarantees regarding taxation, abortion and military neutrality. The amendment was passed with a 67.1% Yes / 32.9% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-eighth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 28th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Treaty of Lisbon. The amendment was rejected with a 46.6% Yes / 53.4% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-eighth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2008

text: Referendum held on the 27th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which limits the right to citizenship at birth to people born on the island of Ireland to at least one parent who is or is entitled to be an Irish citizen. The amendment was passed with a 79.2% Yes / 20.8% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-seventh Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 26th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Treaty of Nice. Following the rejection of the similar amendment the year prior, this amendment also added a clause barring Ireland from joining an EU common defence, in keeping with Ireland’s policy of military neutrality. The amendment was passed with a 62.9% Yes / 37.1% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-sixth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 25th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have (much like the failed 12th amendment) removed the threat of suicide as a grounds for legal abortion and added penalties for performing or assisting abortions. The amendment was rejected with a 49.6% Yes / 50.4% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twenty-fifth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2001

text: Referendum held on the 20th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which constitutionally recognised local government for the first time and added a five year limit for local elections. The amendment was passed with a 77.8% Yes / 22.2% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twentieth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 18th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Treaty of Amsterdam. The amendment was passed with a 61.7% Yes / 38.3% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Eighteenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 19th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the British–Irish Agreement, which makes up part of the Good Friday Agreement. The amendment was passed with a 94.4% Yes / 5.6% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Nineteenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 17th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which added an exception to cabinet confidentiality for cases where the High Court determines that disclosure should be made for the sake of a court’s interest or public interest. The amendment was passed with a 52.6% Yes / 47.4% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Seventeenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 16th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which explicitly permits laws for the refusal of bail in order to prevent commission of serious offences. The amendment was passed with a 74.8% Yes / 25.2% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Sixteenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 15th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which removed the ban on divorce (also providing specific conditions, different to those of the failed 10th amendment, where divorce was allowed). The amendment was passed with a 50.3% Yes / 49.7% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fifteenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 13th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which stated that the prohibition of abortion did not limit foreign travel. The amendment was passed with a 62.4% Yes / 37.6% No vote.

Referendum held on a potential 12th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have removed the threat of suicide as a grounds for legal abortion. The amendment was rejected with a 34.6% Yes / 65.4% No vote.

Referendum held on the 14th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which stated that there was no limit to obtaining or making available information on abortion services in foreign countries. The amendment was passed with a 59.9% Yes / 40.1% No vote.
Referendum held on the 11th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Maastricht Treaty. The amendment was passed with a 69.1% Yes / 30.9% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Eleventh Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 10th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permitted Ireland’s ratification of the Single European Act. The amendment was passed with a 69.9% Yes / 30.1% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tenth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 10th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have removed the ban on divorce (also providing specific conditions where divorce was allowed). The amendment was rejected with a 36.5% Yes / 63.5% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tenth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 1986

text: Referendum held on the 9th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which permits non-Irish citizens to vote in general elections. The amendment was passed with a 75.4% Yes / 24.6% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Ninth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 8th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which guaranteed the unborn the right to life. The amendment was passed with a 66.9% Yes / 33.1% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Eighth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 7th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland, which explicitly permits the alteration of the Seanad’s university constituencies. The amendment was passed with a 92.4% Yes / 7.6% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Seventh Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 6th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland, which ensured that certain adoption orders could not be considered unconstitutional. The amendment was passed with a 99.0% Yes / 1.0% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Sixth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 4th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland, which lowered the minimum voting age from 21 to 18. The amendment was passed with a 84.6% Yes / 15.4% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fourth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 5th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland, which removed the special recognition of the Catholic Church and the additional recognition of other named religious denominations. The amendment was passed with a 84.4% Yes / 15.6% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fifth Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on the 3rd amendment to the Constitution of Ireland, which permitted Ireland’s entry into the European Communities and allowed European Communities law to take precedence over constitutional law. The amendment was passed with a 83.1% Yes / 16.9% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Third Amendment of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Referendum held on a potential 3rd amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have made the rules regarding Dáil constituencies’ ratio of population to TDs more lenient. The amendment was rejected with a 39.2% Yes / 60.8% No vote.

Referendum held on a potential 4th amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which, much like the 1959 failed 3rd amendment, would have switched the general election voting system from PR-STV to first-past-the-post. The amendment was rejected with a 39.2% Yes / 60.8% No vote.

Referendum held on a potential 3rd amendment to the Constitution of Ireland which would have switched the general election voting system from PR-STV to first-past-the-post. The amendment was rejected with a 48.2% Yes / 51.8% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Third Amendment of the Constitution Bill 1958

text: Plebiscite held on the adoption of the Constitution of Ireland, which replaced the Constitution of the Irish Free State. The constitution was adopted with a 56.5% Yes / 43.5% No vote.

links.label: Wikipedia: Adoption of the Constitution of Ireland

text: Election for the successor to Michael D. Higgins’s first term, triggered due to the end of said term. Higgins ran for a second term as an independent (having left Labour upon being elected) and was re-elected with 55.8% of the vote.

Election for the 9th president of Ireland, triggered due to the end of Mary McAleese’s second term. Labour candidate Michael D. Higgins was elected with 39.6% of first preference votes and 56.8% of final count votes.

Election for the 8th president of Ireland, triggered due to Mary Robinson resigning to assume the post of United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. Fianna Fáil candidate Mary McAleese (also supported by the Progressive Democrats) was elected with 45.2% of first preference votes and 55.6% of final count votes. McAleese was elected unopposed for a second term in 2004.

Election for the 7th president of Ireland, triggered due to the end of Patrick Hillery’s second term. Mary Robinson, an independent candidate nominated by the Labour Party (and also supported by the Workers’ Party and Green Party), was elected with 38.9% of first preference votes and 51.9% of final count votes.

Election for the 4th president of Ireland, triggered due to the end of Eamon de Valera’s second term. Fianna Fáil candidate Erskine H. Childers was elected with 52.0% of the vote. In November 1974, Childers died in office and Fianna Fáil candidate Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh was elected unopposed as the 5th president of Ireland. In October 1976, Ó Dálaigh resigned due to a falling out between himself and the Fine Gael–Labour government and Fianna Fáil candidate Patrick Hillery was elected unopposed as the 6th president of Ireland. Hillery was elected unopposed for a second term in 1983.
Election for the successor to Eamon de Valera’s first term, triggered due to the end of said term. De Valera ran for a second term and was re-elected with 50.5% of the vote.

Election for the 3rd president of Ireland, triggered due to the end of Seán T. O’Kelly’s second term. Fianna Fáil candidate and then Taoiseach Eamon de Valera was elected with 56.3% of the vote, resigning as Taoiseach to take up the office.

Election for the 2nd president of Ireland, triggered due to the end of Douglas Hyde’s first and only term (Hyde, an independent candidate, was elected unopposed as the 1st president in 1938). Hyde did not seek a second term, and Fianna Fáil candidate Seán T. O’Kelly was elected with 49.5% of first preference votes and 52.0% of final count votes. O’Kelly was elected unopposed for a second term in 1952.
Elections for Ireland’s 31 administrative counties, which had a total of 949 seats. Fianna Fáil won 248 seats (26.1%), Fine Gael won 245 (25.8%) and Sinn Féin won 102 (10.7%).
Elections for Ireland’s 31 administrative counties, which had a total of 949 seats. Fianna Fáil won 279 seats (29.4%), Fine Gael won 255 (26.9%) and Sinn Féin won 81 (8.5%).
Elections for Ireland’s 31 administrative counties, which had a total of 949 seats. Fianna Fáil won 267 seats (28.1%), Fine Gael won 235 (24.8%) and Sinn Féin won 159 (16.8%).
Elections for Ireland’s 34 administrative counties, which had a total of 883 seats. Fine Gael won 340 seats (38.5%), Fianna Fáil won 218 (24.7%) and Labour won 132 (14.9%).
